claim_verdicts.rationale: This is a surviving direct Caroline-to-Darwin response pair. Caroline's body asks for an account of Lyell's speech and questions what is new in Herschel's chronology argument; Darwin's body explicitly identifies both as questions in her last letter and answers them. The 345 editorial apparatus also points directly to the 27 February 1837 letter in footnote 5. XML identities are Caroline Sarah Darwin to Charles Robert Darwin for 345 and Charles Robert Darwin to Caroline Sarah Darwin for 346.

body_editorial_exact_quotes.quote: We are longing to have an account of Lyells speech.
so I do not see how what Sir J Herschell says is new.
You enquired in yr. last letter about Lyell’s Speech;
You tell me you do not see what is new in Sir J. Herschell’s idea about the chronology of the old Testament being wrong.
See letter to Caroline Darwin, 27 February 1837, n. 5.

caveats: 27 February is Darwin's resolved outgoing date and establishes that 345 was available to him by then; 345's 21 February composition/sent date is not a receipt or knowledge date, and actual delivery remains unknown.

346 is a copy (C 4pp), with the copyist's date corrected from 29 to 27 February and a transcription lacuna in the phrase about the Chinese and Caucasian languages. The response identification survives those source limitations.
The incoming 345 body is Caroline's voice; only 346 supplies Darwin's response voice. Preserve the transcription and section boundaries if exporting.

claim_verdicts.rationale: This is a surviving direct Emma-to-Darwin response pair. Emma's 444 discusses Caroline Tollet's reading and the unresolved central-versus-suburban housing choice; Darwin's 445 acknowledges getting her letter and answers both distinctive topics, including the Tollet reading and her oscillating housing opinion. XML identities are Emma Wedgwood to Charles Robert Darwin for 444 and Charles Robert Darwin to Emma Wedgwood for 445.

body_editorial_exact_quotes.quote: Caroline Tollet says in her situation she finds she can read nothing but sermons & Nicholas Nickleby.
Elizabeth & Caroline are grown suburban again & it is very puzzling
I was very glad to get your letter;
You say Caroline Tollet has two works to read, & that you could read one, if not already read,
I am glad to hear you are oscillating in opinion,
Responds to items in CD’s letter, just received.

caveats: 444 has mutually exclusive XML alternatives of 25 or 26 November 1838 and a Sunday/Monday internal sequence; neither date is a receipt date. Darwin's resolved 27 November outgoing date establishes availability by 27 November, while actual delivery remains unlocated.
444's postmark is 27 November, and 445 is bracket-dated 27 November; these facts do not establish a same-day delivery or exact writing order beyond the response evidence in 445.

445 is an original letter with an editorially supplied bracketed date and a cut-off postscript to Francis Wedgwood. That postscript is not part of the surviving body supplied here. The incoming 444 body is Emma's voice; only 445 supplies Darwin's response voice.

rejected_claim_verdicts.rationale: Reject 441 as the identified direct prompt for 445. 441 is Emma's 21–22 November letter and contains a request about the farewell discourse plus cover notes for a next Darwin letter that the editorial apparatus says is now lost. 444, the later Emma letter, contains the exact Tollet and housing material answered by 445. Its footnote separately identifies Darwin's response to Emma's 21–22 November letter as missing. Therefore topic overlap through the same correspondent cannot replace the missing 441 response or make 441 the direct source of 445.

body_editorial_exact_quotes.quote: Will you do me a favour? yes I am sure you will
The notes were made for subjects to be discussed in CD’s next letter to Emma, now lost
CD’s letter written in response to Emma’s of [21–2 November 1838] is missing.
Caroline Tollet says in her situation she finds she can read nothing but sermons & Nicholas Nickleby.
You say Caroline Tollet has two works to read, & that you could read one, if not already read,

caveats: Rejection concerns 441 as the identified direct prompt for 445; it does not claim that 441 was unread or undelivered, nor that the missing Darwin reply can be reconstructed.
The 21–22 November range and the missing intervening Darwin letter must remain explicit. No incoming Emma text is evidence of Darwin's voice.
